summary: This document gives best current practice for dropping or marking packets with any active queue management (AQM) algorithm, including RED, BLUE, PCN, CoDel, and PIE. It addresses whether congestion signals should depend on packet size or count.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router's queue is full it has to drop or mark some packets. This document settles whether the size of a packet should affect that choice. The answer is that the network should treat all packets alike, and only the sending transport should take the size of the lost packet into account.

subtitle: Should a congested router treat small and large packets differently when it drops or marks them? This BCP says no.

tldr.problem: When a router queue overflows it must drop or mark packets, and it was never settled whether the chance of dropping a packet should depend on how big that packet is. Small packets dropped less often look attractive, because fewer control packets are lost.
tldr.mechanism: The document separates three stages. The queue is measured in bytes or in packets depending on what congests the resource. The drop or mark decision must not depend on the size of the packet. The transport, in turn, should scale its rate reduction by the size of the packet it lost.
tldr.outcome: Dropping small packets less often is deprecated, because it rewards transports for sending tiny segments and helps a flood of small packets push real traffic out of the way. It updates RFC 2309 and adds to the congestion control principles of RFC 2914.

today: RFC 7141 is BCP 41, a Best Current Practice from February 2014. It updates RFC 2309 and RFC 2914, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Three Stages of Congestion Notification
sections.content:
The document gives best current practice for how congestion control functions should scale with packet size for the long term, and it recognises that expediency may be necessary to deal with existing widely deployed protocols that do not live up to the long-term goal.

One reason active queue management was originally introduced was to reduce the lock-out effect that small packets can have on large packets in tail-drop queues. The question of whether to take packet size into account arises at three stages. When measuring congestion, a congested resource asks whether it should measure its queue length in time, in bytes or in packets. When encoding a congestion notification into the wire protocol, a congested resource asks whether the probability that it drops or marks each packet should depend on the size of that packet. When decoding a notification, a transport asks whether it should take into account the size of each missing or marked packet.

Consensus had emerged on the first stage: if possible it is best to measure congestion by time in the queue, and otherwise the choice between bytes and packets depends only on whether the resource is congested by bytes or by packets. The controversy was around the last two stages. The RFC series had been silent other than a paper trail of advice that conditionally recommended byte-mode, packet-size dependent drop.

Reducing the number of small packets dropped has tempting advantages: it drops fewer control packets, which tend to be small, and it makes TCP's bit rate less dependent on packet size. But there are ways of addressing these at the transport layer, rather than reverse engineering network forwarding to fix the problems.

The memo updates RFC 2309 to deprecate deliberate preferential treatment of packets in AQM algorithms solely because of their size, and it adds to the congestion control principles enumerated in BCP 41. In the particular case of Random Early Detection, the byte-mode packet drop variant should not be used to drop fewer small packets, because that creates a perverse incentive for transports to use tiny segments and opens up a denial of service vulnerability. All the RED implementers who responded to the survey in the document had not followed the earlier advice to use byte-mode drop, so the position the memo argues for already existed in implementations. At the transport layer, however, TCP congestion control does not scale with packet size, and the memo recommends that new congestion control mechanisms be built with packet size scaling rather than assuming TCP's example should be followed.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three separate questions here: how a router measures how full its queue is, how it decides which packets to drop, and how the sender reacts to a loss. The first was already settled. The document settles the other two, and it says the fix belongs in the sender rather than in the network.

sections.title: Bit-Congestible and Packet-Congestible Resources
sections.content:
Congestion notification is a changing signal that aims to communicate the probability that the network resource or resources will not be able to forward the level of traffic load offered, or that there is an impending risk that they will not be able to. The qualifier is there because AQM systems set a virtual limit smaller than the actual limit of the resource, then notify the transport when that virtual limit is exceeded, to avoid uncontrolled congestion of the actual capacity. Congestion notification communicates a real number bounded by the range 0 to 1, which ties in with the best-understood measure of it, the drop probability.

The byte against packet dilemma concerns congestion notification whether it is signalled implicitly by drop or explicitly using ECN or PCN. Throughout the document the term marking means notifying congestion explicitly, and congestion notification means notifying it either implicitly by drop or explicitly by marking.

If the load on a resource depends on the rate at which packets arrive it is called packet-congestible; if it depends on the rate at which bits arrive it is called bit-congestible. Examples of packet-congestible resources are route look-up engines and firewalls, because the load depends on how many packet headers they have to process. Examples of bit-congestible resources are transmission links, radio power, and most buffer memory, because the load depends on how many bits they have to transmit or store. Some machine architectures use fixed-size packet buffers, in which case buffer memory is packet-congestible.

The path through a machine typically encounters both kinds of resource. However, a design goal of network processing equipment such as routers and firewalls is to size the packet-processing engines relative to the lines, to keep packet processing uncongested even under worst-case packet rates with runs of minimum-size packets, so packet congestion is currently rare, though there is no guarantee that it will not become more common.

Resources may be congestible at a coarser granularity than bits or packets: stateful firewalls are flow-congestible and call-servers are session-congestible. The memo focuses on congestion of connectionless resources, but says the same principles may apply to protocols controlling per-flow and per-session processing.

In RED, whether the queue is measured in packets or in bytes is called packet-mode or byte-mode queue measurement, and whether the probability of dropping a particular packet depends on its size is called packet-mode or byte-mode drop. The terms byte-mode and packet-mode should not be used without saying which of the two they apply to.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of bottleneck matter. A link or a buffer is slowed down by the number of bits it has to move, so it should be measured in bytes. A firewall or a routing lookup is slowed down by the number of packets it has to look at, so it should be measured in packets. Measuring a queue in the wrong unit hides the real bottleneck.

sections.title: Packet-Mode Drop Against Byte-Mode Drop
sections.content:
The RFC compares how packet-mode and byte-mode drop affect two flows of different packet sizes, giving the expected number of packets and of bits dropped in one second. Each example flow runs at the same bit rate of 48 Mbps, but one is broken into small 60 byte packets and the other into large 1,500 byte packets.

To keep up the same bit rate there are about 25 times more small packets in one second, because they are 25 times smaller: 100,000 small packets per second against 4,000 large packets per second.

For packet-mode drop, the example uses a drop probability of 0.1%, applied to all packets irrespective of size. Because there are 25 times more small packets, it drops 25 times more small packets: 100 small packets but only 4 large packets. Counting bits, however, there are 48,000 bits in the 100 small packets and 48,000 bits in the 4 large packets, the same number. The packet-mode drop algorithm drops any bit with the same probability whether the bit is in a small or a large packet.

For byte-mode drop, the example again uses a drop probability of 0.1%, but only for maximum size packets, assuming a link maximum transmission unit of 1,500 bytes or 12,000 bits. The byte-mode algorithm reduces the drop probability of smaller packets in proportion to their size, making the probability that it drops a small packet 25 times smaller, at 0.004%. There are 25 times more small packets, so dropping them with 25 times lower probability results in dropping the same number of packets: 4 in both cases. But the 4 small dropped packets contain 25 times fewer bits than the 4 large dropped packets, 1,920 compared to 48,000. The byte-mode drop algorithm drops any bit with a probability proportionate to the size of the packet it is in.
sections.plainLanguage: Two flows carry the same 48 Mbps all second. One uses 60-byte packets, so it sends 100,000 of them; the other uses 1,500-byte packets, so it sends 4,000. Dropping every packet with the same chance loses the same number of bits from both flows. Dropping small packets with a proportionally lower chance loses far fewer bits from the small-packet flow.

sections.title: Recommendation on Queue Measurement
sections.content:
Ideally an AQM would measure the service time of the queue. Service time can only be measured as packets leave the queue, where it is not always expedient to implement a full AQM algorithm, so to predict the service time as packets join the queue the algorithm needs to measure the length of the queue.

If the resource is bit-congestible, the implementation should measure the length of the queue in bytes, and if it is packet-congestible it should measure it in packets. Subject to the exceptions, no other choice makes sense, because the number of packets waiting in the queue is not relevant if the resource gets congested by bytes, and the reverse holds as well. The length of the queue into a transmission line would be measured in bytes, while the length of the queue into a firewall would be measured in packets. To avoid the pathological effects of tail drop, the AQM can then transform this service time or queue length into the probability of dropping or marking a packet, for example RED's piecewise linear function between thresholds.

For RED specifically, an implementation should use byte-mode queue measurement for bit-congestible resources and packet-mode queue measurement for packet-congestible ones, and should not make it possible to configure the way a queue measures itself, because whether a queue is bit-congestible or packet-congestible is an inherent property of the queue. Exceptions may be necessary, for instance where a packet-congestible resource has to be configured as a proxy bottleneck for a bit-congestible resource in an adjacent box that does not support AQM.

The less straightforward scenarios are discussed later in the document. Section 4.1.1 explains that the queue into a line should be measured in bytes even if the queue consists of fixed-size packet buffers, because the root cause of the congestion is bytes arriving too fast for the line, and packets filling buffers are merely a symptom of the underlying congestion of the line.
sections.plainLanguage: Measure the queue in the unit that matches what is actually filling it. A link's queue is measured in bytes and a firewall's queue in packets. Making this a configuration choice is discouraged, because the nature of the bottleneck is a property of the equipment, not a setting.

sections.title: Recommendation on Encoding Congestion Notification
sections.content:
When encoding congestion notification, by drop, ECN or PCN, the probability that network equipment drops or marks a particular packet should not depend on the size of the packet. As the worked example shows, to drop any bit with probability 0.1% it is only necessary to drop every packet with probability 0.1% without regard to the size of each packet. This ensures the network layer offers sufficient congestion information for all known and future transport protocols, and ensures no perverse incentives are created that would encourage transports to use inappropriately small packet sizes.

For RED specifically, the algorithm should not use byte-mode drop and ought to use packet-mode drop, because byte-mode drop is more complex, creates the perverse incentive to fragment segments into tiny pieces, and is vulnerable to floods of small packets. If a vendor has implemented byte-mode drop and an operator has turned it on, it is recommended that the operator use packet-mode drop instead, after establishing whether there are implications for the relative performance of applications using different packet sizes. The unlikely possibility of an application-specific legacy use of byte-mode drop is the only reason the recommendations are not phrased more strongly.

RED as a whole should not be switched off, because without it a tail-drop queue biases against large packets and is vulnerable to floods of small packets. The memo warns against confusing RED's byte-mode queue drop, which is completely orthogonal to byte-mode queue measurement: an implementation that has a byte mode but does not say which kind of byte mode is most probably using byte-mode queue measurement, which is fine, and if in doubt the vendor should be consulted. A survey in Appendix A showed that there appears to be little, if any, installed base of the byte-mode drop variant, which suggests that deprecating it will have little, if any, incremental deployment impact.
sections.plainLanguage: When the router decides to drop or mark, it should not look at how big the packet is. Every packet gets the same chance. The memo adds that RED itself should stay in use, because the older tail-drop queue it replaced was worse in other ways.

sections.title: Recommendation on Responding to Congestion
sections.content:
When a transport detects that a packet has been lost or congestion marked, it should consider the strength of the congestion indication as proportionate to the size in octets of the missing or marked packet. In other words, a packet that indicates congestion, by being lost or marked, can be considered conceptually as if there were a congestion indication on every octet of the packet, not just one indication per packet. The recommendation describes only how a transport should interpret the meaning of a congestion indication, as a long-term goal; it makes no recommendation on whether a transport should act differently on the basis of that interpretation, and it merely aids interoperability between transports that do so.

For TCP, if two flows with different packet sizes are required to run at equal bit rates under the same path conditions, this should be done by altering TCP rather than network equipment, because the latter affects other transports besides TCP. If it is desired to improve TCP performance by reducing the chance that a SYN or a pure ACK is dropped, that too should be done by modifying TCP rather than network equipment. The memo is not recommending that TCPs under equivalent conditions should aim for equal bit rates; it says that anyone trying to do such a thing should modify their TCP algorithm, not the network. The recommendations are phrased as should rather than must because there may be cases where expediency dictates that compatibility with pre-existing versions of a transport protocol makes them impractical.

Packets carrying congestion indications may be split or merged in some circumstances, for example at an RTP or RTCP transcoder or during IP fragment reassembly, and splitting and merging only make sense in the context of ECN, not loss. The general rule is that the number of octets in packets with congestion indications should be equivalent before and after merging or splitting, which follows from the principle that an indication of congestion on a packet can be considered an indication on each octet of the packet. The rule is not phrased with must, to allow for protocols that were not designed to conserve congestion-marked octets, such as IP fragment reassembly or loss statistics in RTCP receiver reports before ECN was added. When such a protocol is updated it should comply with the rule, although the rule may be relaxed if it would otherwise become too complex to interoperate with pre-existing implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender is where packet size belongs. If a 1,500-byte packet is lost, the sender should cut its rate as if that many bytes had been signalled, not as if a single small event had happened. And when a marked packet is split or joined with others, the marked octets should be conserved across the split.

sections.title: Why the Network Should Not Favour Small Packets
sections.content:
A protocol design must take care not to cause unintended consequences by giving the parties in the exchange perverse incentives. There are many good reasons why larger path maximum transmission units would help solve scaling issues, so no bias against large packets should be created that is greater than their true cost.

A queue that gives an advantage to small packets can be used to amplify the force of a flooding attack: by sending a flood of small packets, an attacker can get the queue to discard more large-packet traffic, so more attack traffic gets through to cause further damage. Even without malice, if it is noticed that small packets tend to go faster, designers will act in their own interest and use smaller packets. Queues that give advantage to small packets create an evolutionary pressure for applications or transports to send at the same bit rate but break their data stream into tiny segments to reduce their drop rate, and a high volume of tiny packets might in turn unnecessarily overload an unrelated part of the system that is more limited by header processing than by bandwidth.

The RFC works this through with two unresponsive flows at a bit-congestible transmission link, each at 1 Mbps, one using 1,500-byte packets and the other 60-byte packets. With the byte-mode drop variant of RED configured, the algorithm aims to drop 25 times more of the larger packets than the smaller ones, so if it drops 25% of the larger packets it aims to drop 1% of the smaller ones. Even though both flows arrive at the same bit rate, the bit rate the RED queue aims to pass to the line is 750 kbps for the flow of larger packets but 990 kbps for the smaller one. The memo also notes that tail-drop queues amplify small-packet attacks even more, and that wherever possible neither should be used.

A second argument is that small is not the same as control. Dropping fewer control packets considerably improves performance, and it is tempting to drop small packets with lower probability because many control packets tend to be smaller, such as TCP SYNs and ACKs, DNS queries and responses, SIP messages and HTTP GETs. But control packets must not be given preference purely by virtue of their smallness, otherwise it is too easy for any data source to get the same preferential treatment simply by sending data in smaller packets. Just because many control packets are small does not mean all small packets are control packets. The argument is that the transport should be made more robust against losses of control packets, rather than fixing this in the network.

A third argument is a transport-independent network. TCP congestion control ensures that flows competing for the same resource each maintain the same number of segments in flight, irrespective of segment size, so under similar conditions flows with different segment sizes get different bit rates.
sections.plainLanguage: Favouring small packets looks harmless and is not. It rewards applications for breaking their data into tiny pieces, and it lets an attacker flood a queue with small packets so that more of the real traffic is discarded. Control packets are often small, but the answer is to make the sender robust to losing a control packet, not to make the network prefer small ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo recommends that queues do not bias drop probability due to packet size. Dropping small packets less often than large ones creates a perverse incentive for transports to break their flows into tiny segments. One of the benefits of implementing AQM was meant to be to remove this perverse incentive that tail-drop queues gave to small packets.

In practice, transports cannot all be trusted to respond to congestion, so another reason for recommending that queues not bias drop probability towards small packets is to avoid the vulnerability to small-packet denial of service attacks that would otherwise result. One of the benefits of implementing AQM was meant to be to remove tail drop's vulnerability to small packets, so it should not be added back again.

If most queues implemented AQM with byte-mode drop, the resulting network would amplify the potency of a small-packet denial of service attack. At the first queue, the stream of packets would push aside a greater proportion of large packets, so more of the small packets would survive to attack the next queue, and the flood would continue on towards the destination, pushing regular traffic with large packets out of the way one queue after another while suffering much less drop itself.

The appendix on byte-mode drop explains why the ability of networks to police the response of any transport to congestion depends on bit-congestible network resources only doing packet-mode drop. Making the drop probability depend on the size of the packets that bits happen to be divided into simply encourages the bits to be divided into smaller packets, and byte-mode drop would therefore irreversibly complicate any attempt to fix the Internet's incentive structures.
sections.plainLanguage: A queue that spares small packets lets a flood of small packets push large, ordinary traffic out of the way at every queue along the path. The memo's rule is meant to stop that, and to stop applications being pushed towards sending ever smaller packets.

viz.caption: The three stages and the answer for each

items.title: Measuring the queue
items.text: It depends. Count in bytes if the resource is congested by bytes, in packets if it is congested by packets, and in time if that is feasible.

items.title: Encoding the notification
items.text: No. The probability that a packet is dropped or marked should not depend on the size of that packet.

items.title: Responding to the notification
items.text: Yes. The strength of the transport's rate reduction should be proportionate to the size of the packet that was lost or marked.

viz.caption: The terms the document sorts out

items.title: Bit-congestible
items.text: A resource whose load depends on the rate at which bits arrive: transmission links, radio power and most buffer memory.

items.title: Packet-congestible
items.text: A resource whose load depends on the rate at which packets arrive: route look-up engines and firewalls.

items.title: Byte-mode queue measurement
items.text: Measuring the length of a queue in bytes. Appropriate for a bit-congestible resource.

items.title: Byte-mode drop
items.text: Dropping a packet with a probability that depends on its size. The memo recommends against it.

items.title: Explicit and implicit notification
items.text: Marking, whether by ECN or PCN, is explicit notification; dropping a packet is implicit notification.

How to measure the queue in front of each kind of resource
What the memo says about RED

items.title: Use packet-mode drop
items.text: The RED algorithm should not use byte-mode drop, because byte-mode drop is more complex, pushes transports towards tiny segments and is vulnerable to floods of small packets.

items.title: Do not switch RED off
items.text: RED as a whole should not be switched off. Without it, a tail-drop queue biases against large packets and is vulnerable to floods of small packets.

items.title: Byte-mode measurement is fine
items.text: Byte-mode queue drop is completely orthogonal to byte-mode queue measurement, and byte-mode measurement is often the right choice.

items.title: Operators should switch
items.text: Where byte-mode drop has been implemented and turned on, the operator is recommended to use packet-mode drop instead, after checking the effect on applications using different packet sizes.

items.title: Small packets push others out
items.text: A queue that drops large packets more often than small ones lets a flood of small packets displace the traffic that matters.

items.title: It compounds along the path
items.text: At each queue in turn, the flood survives better than the large packets it displaces, so it reaches the destination while ordinary traffic does not.

items.title: AQM was meant to fix this
items.text: Removing the bias against large packets was one of the reasons for introducing active queue management, so byte-mode drop would put it back.

items.title: It pushes transports the wrong way
items.text: Favouring small packets rewards transports for fragmenting their data into tiny segments, and byte-mode drop would make that incentive hard to undo.
